questions.q: What does a Glue crawler actually do to your data?
options: It samples the data to infer schema and format, then writes table metadata to the Data Catalog — it never transforms or moves the underlying files
It transforms and rewrites every file it scans into Parquet
It deletes files that don't match the expected schema
It copies all scanned data into a new S3 bucket
questions.explain: A crawler is a metadata-only operation. It reads samples to infer schema and format, then writes or updates Data Catalog table entries.

questions.q: What is a classifier in AWS Glue?
options: Logic (built-in or custom) that detects a data source's format and helps infer schema
The compute unit Glue jobs are billed in
A type of Glue trigger that starts crawlers
An IAM policy attached to a crawler role
questions.explain: Classifiers detect format — Parquet, CSV, JSON, and so on — and Glue ships built-in ones plus support for custom classifiers like grok patterns.

questions.q: What happens when a crawler runs again after new files with an added column have landed under an existing table's prefix?
options: It can detect the schema change and update the existing table definition rather than creating a duplicate
It always fails and requires the table to be deleted manually first
It silently ignores the new column forever
It automatically deletes the older files that lack the new column
questions.explain: Crawlers can detect schema changes on rerun and update the existing Data Catalog table definition.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the crawler scheduling options this lesson describes?
options: Continuous streaming mode with sub-second latency
On demand — triggered manually or by another process
On a schedule, using a cron-like expression
Chained into a workflow after an upstream job
questions.explain: The lesson describes on-demand, scheduled, and workflow-chained crawler runs — not a continuous streaming mode.

questions.q: Why does a crawler potentially create multiple tables from data under a single S3 prefix?
options: If it finds multiple distinct schemas under that prefix, it may create separate tables for each
Crawlers always create exactly one table per S3 bucket, never per prefix
It creates a new table every time it runs, regardless of schema
It only happens when the data is stored in JSON format
questions.explain: Inconsistent schemas under the same prefix can lead a crawler to create separate tables, which is why a clean, deliberate key layout matters.
